articles.title: Immanuel Kant, filósofo: "El cielo estrellado sobre mí y la ley moral dentro de mí llenan el ánimo de admiración y respeto siempre nuevos y crecientes"
articles.standfirst: La ética kantiana nos enseña que actuar por deber puede guiarnos a la responsabilidad en decisiones difíciles, un recurso invaluable ante los dilemas cotidianos que enfrentamos en nuestra vida personal y profesional.
articles.summary: La ética kantiana nos enseña que actuar por deber puede guiarnos a la responsabilidad en decisiones difíciles, un recurso invaluable ante los dilemas cotidianos que enfrentamos en nuestra vida personal y profesional.
articles.body: La búsqueda de sentido y dirección en la vida es una preocupación común en la experiencia humana. Sentirse perdido, anhelando la aprobación de los demás o lidiando con la soledad, son luchas cotidianas que nos dejan un vacío existencial. Esta situación se agudiza cuando nos enfrentamos al miedo de equivocarnos, llevando a la frustración y a la incapacidad de disfrutar del presente. En este contexto, Kant sugiere que la admiración por el cosmos y la ley moral que habita dentro de nosotros pueden proporcionar una guía, implicando que una vida íntegra puede y debe ser moralmente orientada. En su obra 'Crítica de la razón práctica', Kant invita a reflexionar sobre cómo la razón y la moralidad deben ser la brújula de nuestras decisiones. A medida que confrontamos la inquietud del futuro y las relaciones difíciles, la idea de que hay un deber moral inherente a nuestra existencia puede ofrecernos un camino hacia una felicidad más duradera, distante de las expectativas externas y anclada en nuestro propio sentido del deber. Para comprender el problema de los dilemas éticos en entornos laborales y decisiones personales difíciles, el pensamiento de Immanuel Kant ofrece una perspectiva especialmente interesante. Su reflexión sobre la ética kantiana y el imperativo categórico plantea que un acto moral debe ser realizado por deber y que la razón nos guía a imponer leyes morales universales, fundamentalizando la moralidad sin depender de consecuencias empíricas. Immanuel Kant (1724-1804) fue un filósofo prusiano, destacado como uno de los máximos exponentes de la Ilustración. Su pensamiento revolucionó la filosofía moderna, centrándose en cuestiones fundamentales como el conocimiento, la moral y la política. A lo largo de su vida, Kant trabajó como profesor de Lógica y Metafísica en la Universidad de Königsberg, donde desarrolló ideas que aún son objeto de estudio y debate, como el imperativo categórico, que sostiene que las acciones morales deben ser realizadas por deber, independientemente de sus consecuencias. El contexto intelectual de Kant es clave para entender su pensamiento. Enfrentó y se vio influenciado por las obras de pensadores como David Hume, a quien respondió al redefinir la teoría del conocimiento. A lo largo de su carrera, Kant creó un puente entre el empirismo y el racionalismo, desarrollando el idealismo trascendental, que propuso que el conocimiento surge de nuestra experiencia, pero está condicionado por estructuras a priori de la mente. Este enfoque lo posicionó en una corriente filosófica que influiría en muchos autores posteriores, como Hegel y Schopenhauer, quienes expandieron y reinterpretaron sus ideas.

articles.title: 2026 Nobel Peace Prize awarded to Navi Pillay
articles.summary: Pillay, 85, has been instrumental in ensuring war crimes and genocide are prosecuted, Nobel committee says.
articles.body:
The Norwegian Nobel Committee has awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize to Navanethem “Navi” Pillay.

The committee’s announcement of the 125th Nobel Peace Prize, made on Friday in Oslo, said the award would go to the South African jurist for her work to promote peace and international law.

It added that Pillay, a former United Nations high commissioner for human rights, had been instrumental in ensuring war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide are prosecuted.

“At a time of existential challenges – including more wars and conflicts than the world has seen in a long time – international law is no longer just a supplement to peace and security. It is an absolute necessity,” the committee said in a statement.

Committee Chairman Jorgen Watne Frydnes said the system of international law was “under tremendous pressure” and its institutions were “under attack”. It is judges, he continued, “who guard the thin red line between order and chaos”.

Reacting to her Nobel win, Pillay, 85, said she would “dedicate this award to all of the survivors of international crimes”.

She made her statement in the historic courtroom in Germany’s Nuremberg where the trials prosecuting Nazi leaders after World War II were held.

“Perhaps it was meant to be that I was in this historic courtroom … when the announcement was made, and I was informed of the award,” Pillay said.

She also drew attention to UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, which she chaired. It concluded last year that Israel was responsible for genocide in Gaza with a specific intent to destroy Palestinians in Gaza.

“The last thing I did is the delivery of the report on Gaza, naming what’s happening there as genocide,” Pillay said on Friday. “One of the main reactions to that report is paying tribute to me for my courage. And you can imagine how surprised I was. Why would you need courage to speak the truth?”

‘A tribute’ to those defending international law

A South African of Indian Tamil origin, the 85-year-old Pillay was the first woman to start a law practice in what was then the province of Natal in 1967.

She was a defence lawyer for Nelson Mandela, who previously won the Nobel Peace Prize, and other anti-apartheid activists and was the first woman of colour to serve on South Africa’s High Court.

She later served on the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda and the International Criminal Court and as the UN’s rights chief.

The committee highlighted her role during her time on the Rwanda tribunal in establishing that rape and sexual violence can constitute crimes against humanity and genocide.

Her work on the UN inquiry on the occupied Palestinian territory said last year that Israel’s president, prime minister and former defence minister had “incited the commission” of genocide.

“We concluded that the State of Israel is responsible for the commission of four genocidal acts in Gaza with the specific intent to destroy Palestinians in Gaza,” she declared in a presentation to the UN General Assembly at the time.

Reacting to Pillay’s Nobel win, Israel’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs in a post on X on Friday, called it “the grotesque weaponisation of an award to legitimise anti-Israel hatred and prejudice”.

Pillay currently sits on the International Court of Justice in the case in which Myanmar stands accused of genocide against the Rohingya.

“Today’s prize is a tribute to all those working to uphold and defend international law, the rule of law and human rights, and secure peace, justice and human dignity,” UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres reacted to the news of Pillay’s success.

South African President Cyril Ramaphosa said the award was a “profound tribute to the veteran jurist’s courage, integrity and lifelong commitment to justice”.

International law ‘under political attack’

The prize, which is worth 12 million Swedish crowns ($1.2m), will be presented in Oslo ‌on ‌December 10 on the anniversary of the death of Swedish industrialist Alfred Nobel, who founded the awards in his 1895 will.

Four other prizes were announced earlier this week for medicine, physics, chemistry and literature.

The Nobel committee received nominations for 287 candidates for this year’s peace prize. Other contenders included the International Space Station, emergency teams in Sudan, children’s advocates in Ukraine and two top international courts.

Ashok Swain, a researcher at Uppsala University in Sweden said that while the prize will not deliver any concrete change on the ground, the messaging of the award to Pillay is key in the current climate.

“International law … was never perfect, but at least some rules were there. Now, it has become a free-for-all, and everyone interprets it the way they want,” he told Al Jazeera.

United States President Donald Trump has long coveted the prize and repeatedly said he deserves it despite starting the ongoing US-Israel war on Iran.

Last year’s winner, Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado, handed her medal to Trump after the US deposed Venezuelan former President Nicholas Maduro in January.

Pillay joked that she might share her prize with the US leader.

“If you clap a little bit more, I may share this prize with Trump,” she said in a video posted on social media by the secretary-general of Amnesty International that showed Pillay being applauded after the announcement of the award.

Hours after Pillay’s victory, US President ⁠Trump shared a post on Truth Social saying the Nobel committee “demeaned” the prize by awarding it to Pillay, as the White House imposed more sanctions on the International Criminal Court.

In Pillay’s comments on Friday, she denounced attacks on international legal institutions.

“We are living through an era when international law and human rights are under significant political attack,” she said. “This worsening reality is particularly visible with the attacks on the International Criminal Court.”

articles.title: Navi Pillay, former UN human rights chief, wins Nobel Peace Prize
articles.summary: Pillay is recognised for her "efforts to promote peace and international law", the Norwegian Nobel Committee says.
articles.body:
Former UN human rights chief and International Court of Justice judge Navi Pillay has been awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize.

The South African judge was recognised "for her efforts to promote peace and international law", which paved the way for a "more comprehensive global legal order", the Nobel committee said.

Pillay, 85, has taken part in high-profile work considering allegations of human rights violations during a decades-long career, including in Rwanda, Myanmar and Gaza.

Her early work included defending anti-apartheid activists in South Africa, and on Friday she became the country's fifth Peace Prize winner - following in the footsteps of Nelson Mandela and Archbishop Desmond Tutu.

Pillay's work had been "instrumental in ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide are prosecuted", said the chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee Jørgen Watne Frydnes.

"Navi Pillay's commitment to universal legal principles and her firm moral compass are constants in a long career," he said.

"At a time of existential challenges - including more wars and conflicts than the world has seen in a long time - international law is no longer just a supplement to peace and security. It is an absolute necessity."

Frydnes said the committee had not been able to notify Pillay that she had won in advance, "so my message to her would be 'if you see a Norwegian number calling, please pick up'".

Shortly afterwards, Pillay reacted to the news from Nuremberg's Palace of Justice by saying "it must be a joke" and thanked those who had gathered to applaud her.

"If you clap a little bit more I may share this prize with Trump," she joked. Last year's winner, Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado, gave her medal to the US president in January as "recognition for his unique commitment with our freedom" .

Pillay dedicated her award to "all the survivors of international crimes" and the practitioners of international justice "whose compassion and courage continue to ensure that impunity will not be allowed to reign".

Navanethem "Navi" Pillay grew up in South Africa during apartheid as a bus driver's daughter in a poor Indian section of Durban.

She went on to become the first woman to establish a law practice in Natal Province in 1967, and later the first non-white woman to be appointed to the country's high court.

Pillay served as a judge on the UN-backed International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda - focused on the 1994 genocide in which 800,000 people were killed - including four years as its president. She was elected to the International Criminal Court in 2003.

From 2021-25, she chaired the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory - a fact-finding body established by the UN Human Rights Council to investigate alleged violations of international law.

The commission concluded that Israel had committed genocidal acts in Gaza and that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, and his former defence minister Yoav Gallant, had "incited the commission of genocide" in their speeches and statements.

The three-member expert panel did not speak officially for the UN and had no legal authority. Israel rejected its findings and accused the three members of the commission of serving as "Hamas proxies".

The panel had previously concluded that Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups committed war crimes and other grave violations of international law on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and another 251 taken hostage. The same report also accused Israel of war crimes.

Reacting to Pillay's award on Friday, Israel's Foreign Ministry said it represented a "grotesque weaponisation of an award to legitimise anti-Israel hatred and prejudice".

It said in a statement: "Her role in the relentless, politically motivated demonisation of Israel and promotion of the genoLIE speaks volumes."

Frydnes said the Nobel organisation was not taking a position on whether the Israeli offensive in Gaza amounted to genocide.

Pillay is currently a judge on the International Court of Justice (ICJ) in the case where Myanmar stands accused by The Gambia of genocide against the Rohingya people.

Myanmar has denied deliberately trying to destroy the minority Muslim population, with a government representative telling the court in January that the allegation was "unsubstantiated" .

UN human rights chief Volker Turk said Pillay's recognition was "a reaffirmation that human rights, the rule of law and justice, and accountability are fundamental to everything, to peace, to security, and prosperity".

Meanwhile, UN Secretary General António Guterres said she had been "a steadfast, independent voice of justice amidst some of the most historic international legal cases of our time".

South Africa's President Cyril Ramaphosa said she had been a "pioneering defence attorney for anti-apartheid activists" who had worked to "uphold human dignity and bring hope in South Africa and to peoples globally".

Amnesty International secretary general Agnès Callamard said she was with Pillay when she learned she had won - and called her an "inspired choice" for the award.

"At a time when both international law and justice are under attack, when too many states attempt to hollow them out, her Nobel Peace Prize could not come at a better time," she said.

articles.title: I co-created ‘Blues Clues’ — here’s what worries me about today’s content landscape.
articles.summary: Holding a child’s attention is not the same as engaging them.
articles.body:
As a kids’ show creator, I do formative research on every series I make, to ensure that I am meeting my goals — both from an educational and entertainment standpoint. I know how smart kids are, and I want to be sure that I’m putting a show out in the world that elevates kids, empowers them, makes them laugh and gives them something to think about.

But it takes time to make a series this way.

“ Blue’s Clues ” was founded in kindergarten readiness skills — a curriculum we designed to give kids the tools to succeed when they started school. “ Super Why ” was created with a literacy curriculum, to teach kids to learn to read and love to read. “ Daniel Tiger ” was created to showcase socio-emotional skills and to teach kids life lessons. “ Princess Penelope ” was created to teach critical thinking skills and how to solve problems with kindness.

Each of these series has research to prove that we are teaching these skills — and that kids love the shows so much they want them at their birthday parties.

Today, children have access to more content than we could have ever imagined when “Blue’s Clues” premiered in 1996. Some of what is being created for kids today is wonderful. But what worries me most is that too much of it is designed merely to capture children’s attention. Holding children’s attention is not the same as engaging them.

Much of today’s content for kids is candy. Images change quickly. Sounds and colors compete for attention. Loud. Surprising. Inappropriate. A child may stare at the screen, but that doesn’t necessarily mean the content is helping them in any way. Sometimes it simply means the content has been designed to make looking away difficult.

Children deserve more from us than that. No one would ever say that a heavy media diet of candy is good for kids.

When I began working in children’s media, programs were created by teams of writers, educators, researchers, producers and artists. We debated every detail. Would a preschooler understand this word? Was the story moving too quickly? Did we give children enough time to answer? What would they feel when the episode ended?

Today, an algorithm may decide what a child sees next. The algorithm knows what keeps kids watching. Like sugar, it makes them want more. What the algorithm doesn’t know is whether they felt calmer, kinder, more curious or more confident afterward. It doesn’t know if a child is tired, anxious, lonely or overstimulated.

The best children’s content can make a child laugh and give them something useful. It can inspire imaginative play, introduce a new idea or help a child find the words for a feeling they couldn’t explain before. A show for kids should leave something behind after the screen is off.

Parents can ask, How does my child act after watching? Does the program inspire play or conversation? Is my child being invited to think — or only encouraged to keep watching? Does the content respect my child’s intelligence?

The answers matter more than whether a program calls itself educational.

I believe that media can be one of our greatest teaching tools. But technology should serve children. Children should not be used to serve technology.

Angela C. Santomero is the Emmy and Peabody Award-winning co-creator of “Blue’s Clues” and creator of “Daniel Tiger’s Neighborhood,” “Super Why!” and the “Princess Penelope’s Purse of Preposterous Things” book and YouTube series. Her newest books are “ Bunny Lala’s Big Song ” and “ Pirate Argh’s Treasure .”

articles.title: Who is Navi Pillay, winner of the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize?
articles.summary: The 85-year-old South African judge has spent decades fighting apartheid and genocide.
articles.body:
South African judge Navanethem “Navi” Pillay has been awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize, becoming the fifth South African to win it.

Making the announcement on Friday, the Norwegian Nobel Committee praised Pillay for her decades-long efforts to prosecute genocide and war crimes, which have been marked by “judicial rigour, personal integrity and considerable courage”.

From defending activists in apartheid-era South Africa, to more recently overseeing a United Nations inquiry which declared Israel responsible for genocide in Gaza, the 85-year-old, who is also a judge at the International Court of Justice (ICJ), has specialised in international law for decades.

Here’s what we know about her life and why she has been awarded the world’s top peace prize:

Navanethem Pillay, known as Navi Pillay, was born in the racially segregated city of Durban in South Africa’s Natal province in 1940 to parents of Tamil descent.

After earning a law degree from the University of Natal, she became the first woman in Natal province to start her own law firm. Early in her career, she helped defend numerous anti-apartheid activists in the country.

She later became the first woman of colour to sit on the High Court of South Africa. She went on to preside over the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda (ICTR), which prosecuted those charged with humanitarian crimes during the 1994 Rwandan genocide .

Pillay was the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) from 2008 to 2014. More recently she chaired the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory which determined last year that Israel is responsible for carrying out genocide in Gaza .

Currently, Pillay is a judge on the International Court of Justice, acting in a case in which Myanmar is accused of genocide against its mostly Muslim Rohingya minority.

Pillay has spent much of her life advocating for human rights in her home South Africa and abroad. While studying, she took part in boycotts and marches against apartheid. She later joined the legal defence of some of the country’s most prominent anti-apartheid figures, such as Phyllis Naidoo and Strini Moodley.

In 1973, Pillay took on a case that helped secure basic rights, including legal access, for political prisoners on Robben Island, where Nelson Mandela was jailed.

In a 2016 interview with the Diplomatic Courier, Pillay said her early human rights work was “shaped by what (she) had experienced under apartheid”.

“I used many of the challenges to my advantage, I had to learn international humanitarian law so as to defend cases of racial discrimination,” she said.

Pillay oversaw a UN commission of inquiry which concluded in 2025 that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza.

In a statement on the report, Pillay urged UN member states to do everything they can to establish a ceasefire in Gaza and to “ensure justice and accountability for all victims”.

What has she been awarded the Nobel Prize for?

The Nobel committee said Pillay was being honoured for her “efforts to promote peace and international law”.

It called her one of “the great defenders of international legal principles in our time”, having helped hold states and national leaders to account and bring “hope to victims of violence and conflict”.

The committee stressed the role Pillay played in the Rwandan genocide tribunal, saying her influence helped establish “that rape and sexual violence could constitute a crime against humanity – as well as genocide”.

“In the same case, Ms Pillay was instrumental in a separate legal breakthrough: for the first time, a defendant faced charges of incitement to commit genocide purely on the basis of spreading propaganda,” said the committee.

The committee said honouring Pillay is especially important at a time when international law “is under tremendous pressure and its institutions are under attack”.

That message was echoed by rights advocates and international officials.

The UN’s rights chief, Volker Turk, said her award was “a recognition, a reaffirmation that human rights, the rule of law and justice and accountability are fundamental to everything, to peace, to security and prosperity”.

International Criminal Court (ICC) President Tomoko Akane said the award carried special significance “at a time of profound challenges to the international legal order and the rule of law”.

South African President Cyril Ramaphosa praised the award as a tribute to Pillay’s “courage, integrity ⁠⁠⁠⁠and lifelong commitment to justice”.

Haakon Gjerlow, acting director of the Peace Research Institute Oslo, said it “sends a clear message that peace depends not only on political leadership, but on strong, credible international institutions and the courageous people who dedicate their lives to defending them .”

Ashok Swain, a professor of peace and conflict research at Uppsala University, told Al Jazeera that the selection of Pillay was a “pleasant surprise” and the “best possible choice”.

He said the Nobel committee likely took into consideration Pillay’s lifelong record fighting genocide and apartheid. He added that the award to the South African jurist could also be read as a message to United States President Donald Trump, who has long argued that he is deserving of the peace prize and whose administration has clashed with South Africa over debunked claims that white Afrikaners are facing “genocide” .

Furthermore, last year, the Trump administration issued sanctions against members of the ICC in what many critics saw as an attack on the system of international law.

The ICC had previously issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defence Minister Yoav Gallant for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity.

The ICC responded by describing the US sanctions as a “flagrant attack against the independence of an impartial judicial institution” and the victims of war crimes around the world. It said it would continue its work “without regard to any restriction, pressure or threat”.

Pillay appeared to learn of the award as media reports circulated, telling a group of supporters applauding her: “I don’t know about this. So my question is: Is it true?”

She also jokingly referenced Trump, saying, “If you clap a little bit more, I may share this prize with Trump.”

Once the news was confirmed, Pillay said she would dedicate the award to “all of the survivors of international crimes”.

“This award strengthens my conviction that we must ⁠⁠⁠⁠stand together in defence of ⁠⁠⁠⁠the rule of law, in defence of independent ⁠⁠⁠⁠courts and an international ⁠⁠⁠⁠legal order based ⁠⁠⁠⁠on principle.”

Earlier, the Nobel committee said it had struggled to get in touch with Pillay to notify her. “If you see a Norwegian number calling, please pick up,” said committee chair, Jorgen Watne Frydnes.

articles.title: Student loan forgiveness could hike tax bill for borrowers, study finds
articles.summary: A new study says tax bills could triple for people who receive student loan forgiveness through income-driven repayment (IDR) plans. articles.body:
A new study says tax bills could triple for people who receive student loan forgiveness through income-driven repayment (IDR) plans.

Previously, forgiven student loans were exempt from federal income tax, but that provision expired at the end of 2025.

An average married couple with two dependents earning around $60,000 could see their tax bill go up by $7,200, according to Protect Borrowers , a nonprofit group that advocates for debt relief.

Lower-income families, those making around $40,000, would see the biggest increase, with their tax liability growing 11 times their usual rate.

And single borrowers could see 1 out of 4 of their dollars earned go to federal taxes after student loan debt relief through IDR, the study found.

The states that would be hit the hardest, according to the report, are Louisiana, Mississippi, Arkansas, West Virginia, Oklahoma and New Mexico.

“The promise of IDR cancellation has always been a critical aspect of the federal student loan safety net, aimed at ensuring that student loan debt is not a lifelong obligation. However, for decades, IDR cancellation has always come with a catch — a massive tax bill,” the report said.

“Treating such cancelled debt as taxable income will hit many borrowers with an unprecedented tax bomb and force them to replace their debt to the U.S. Department of Education with debt to the Internal Revenue Service (IRS),” it added.

articles.title: Moms for Liberty unleashes AI watchdog on 13,000 school districts to flag controversial policies before votes
articles.summary: Moms for Liberty's new AI tool called M4L AWARE scans school board agendas across 13,000 districts every 12 hours, flagging DEI and gender policies.
articles.body: Moms for Liberty is deploying artificial intelligence to monitor school board agendas across more than 13,000 school districts nationwide, giving parents advance warning about controversial policies before local officials vote on them, Fox News Digital has learned. "The Biden admin targeted our parents for showing up to school board meetings, but we were just getting started," Tina Descovich, Moms for Liberty co-founder and CEO, told Fox News Digital in a statement. "Wait and see what happens when parents receive timely information about what is being discussed at their school board meetings." The new system, dubbed M4L AWARE, which stands for Agenda Watch, Alert, Response, and Engage, scans school board agendas every 12 hours for issues involving diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI), gender policies, curriculum changes and Title IX, according to the parental rights organization. EXCLUSIVE: HOUSE COMMITTEE PROBES CHICAGO PUBLIC SCHOOLS OVER HIDING 'GENDER AFFIRMATION' FROM PARENTS When the system flags a high-priority item, it sends local Moms for Liberty chapters a plain-language summary and a ready-to-share alert designed to help parents organize before a school board meeting. The organization says its system is designed to give chapters a window of roughly 72 hours to mobilize parents, sign up for public comment and scrutinize proposals before board members cast their votes. "Moms for Liberty is harnessing AI to increase the oversight of school boards across the nation, empowering parents like never before," Descovich said. "For five years, we’ve asked parents to show up at school board meetings, and they have. The problem is that it’s incredibly time-consuming to sift through thousands of pages in agendas each week, and school districts count on that." Descovich said the new AI tool will allow Moms for Liberty members and other parents to quickly identify concerning policies buried deep within school board agendas, even when they are released late in the week, giving families time to respond before officials take action. UNEARTHED DOJ EMAILS EXPOSE TURMOIL OVER BIDEN-ERA MEMO URGING CRACKDOWN ON PARENTS The announcement of the tool comes on the heels of a Monday report from the Justice Department's Weaponization Working Group that the FBI opened 25 "Guardian assessments" involving parents following then-Attorney General Merrick Garland's Oct. 4, 2021, memorandum addressing threats against school officials. The report said that an FBI whistleblower disclosed that one mother was investigated following a tip that noted she was a gun owner and belonged to what was described as a "right-wing mom's group." A separate joint DOJ-Education Department release identified that organization as Moms for Liberty. AI IN EDUCATION GIVES US A CHANCE TO USE THE BEST TECH TO FIX OUR BROKEN SCHOOLS CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The Working Group concluded that the memo, according to the DOJ press release, "was the product of pressure exerted by the White House and wrongly weaponized the Department of Justice against parents."

articles.title: In Adani power row, Karnataka Escoms get ₹1,000 crore jolt
articles.summary: Karnataka Escoms face ₹1,000+ crore liability in Adani Power UPCL tariff dispute after SC won’t stay invoices; discoms seek consumer recovery, KERC limits interest.
articles.body: Bengaluru: What began as a tariff dispute with Adani Power-owned Udupi Power Corporation (UPCL) has now become a Rs 1,000-crore-plus liability for Karnataka’s electricity supply companies (Escoms). In August, Supreme Court refused to stay Adani Power’s invoices even as an appeal before Appellate Tribunal for Electricity (APTEL) is pending.UPCL project’s tariff has been locked in litigation and subjected to repeated revisions since 2012. Adani Power had raised a Rs 786-crore claim — Rs 423 crore in carrying cost and Rs 363 crore as accrued interest. Acting on its own reconciliation, Power Company of Karnataka (PCKL) and the discoms disputed the claim, putting the amount payable at Rs 419 crore, including Rs 215 crore towards carrying cost, which they said had already been paid.Discoms have made the payment under protest, while maintaining their legal battle is far from over.Since APTEL is set to pronounce its decision following Supreme Court’s direction, Escoms are hoping Karnataka Electricity Regulatory Commission (KERC) will approve their request to recover the excess payment towards compound interest on the initial tariff amount from electricity consumers.In its Jan 7, 2026 order, Central Electricity Regulatory Commission rejected Karnataka discoms’ argument that carrying cost arising from APTEL’s interim orders could be excluded. It held that successive tariff revisions flowing from APTEL and CERC orders had created differential amounts for which Adani Power was entitled to carrying cost. Energy department sources said that out of the Rs 1,005 crore paid to Adani Power, Bescom alone has paid Rs 456 crore, accounting for 45% of the payout.+++++Tariff pe tariff* In 2010, Central Electricity Regulatory Commission determines provisional and final tariffs for Udupi project* Appellate Tribunal for Electricity, in 2013 and 2014, directs Escoms to pay tariffs and arrears in instalments* Later, CERC revises tariff following APTEL’s final directions, setting off chain of differential payments and carrying-cost claims* At heart of dispute is how much interest discoms must pay on tariff differentials that accumulated as various tariff orders were revised over the years++++++++Who’ll bear Rs 1,005 crore burden?* Bescom has already paid dues to Adani Power and has since recovered it from consumers through Fuel and Power Purchase Cost Adjustment (FPPCA) arrangement levied through monthly electricity bills* Now, Karnataka Electricity Regulatory Commission has refused to validate the entire recovery* Contends Escoms can recover only simple interest, and not compounded interestYou Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Bengaluru | Silver Rate in Bengaluru | Bank Holidays in Bengaluru | Public Holidays in Bengaluru | Bengaluru AQI | Weather in Bengaluru | Petrol Price in Bengaluru | Diesel Price in Bengaluru | CNG Price in Bengaluru | LPG Price in BengaluruStay updated with the latest Bengaluru news. articles.title: Claudia Bavel, "destrozada" después del asesinato a tiros de su cirujano plástico en Marbella: "Era como un padre para mí"
articles.standfirst: La modelo e influencer ha compartido un profundo mensaje en sus redes sociales
articles.summary: La modelo e influencer ha compartido un profundo mensaje en sus redes sociales
articles.body: La modelo e influencer Claudia Bavel, conocida en la prensa del corazón por su pasada relación con el exfutbolista Iker Casillas, se ha mostrado completamente destrozada tras el violento asesinato de su cirujano plástico de confianza, Alexander Aslani, ocurrido el pasado 7 de octubre en la localidad de Marbella. A través de sus redes sociales, la creadora de contenido ha compartido mensajes de dolor en los que asegura tener "el corazón roto" y define al reputado especialista médico como "un padre" para ella. “Tengo el corazón roto. Tenía tanta ilusión de volver a verte cuando viajara a España, me arrepiento tanto de no haber ido a esa revisión antes de volar a República Dominicana. Siempre era un orgullo ser parte de ti y tú de mí. Descansa en paz”, comienza diciendo. “No tengo palabras para describir el dolor que siento. Era un padre para mí, me quería, me respetaba y me apoyaba. Éramos uno. Me quedo con tus últimas palabras: ‘Estoy muy orgulloso de ti’. Juntos hasta el final. Y así será”, añade. La relación de Claudia Bavel y Alexander Aslani surge porque la catalana era una de sus clientas más habituales; de hecho, con él se sometió a intervenciones de implantes mamarios y de glúteos. Alexander Aslani (57 años), prestigioso cirujano plástico de origen alemán asentado en la Costa del Sol, fue asesinado en el interior de la clínica privada Cirumed, en Marbella, establecimiento que dirigía junto a su esposa. Un hombre encapuchado irrumpió en su despacho por la tarde y le descerrajó varios tiros en la cabeza y en el cuello antes de darse a la fuga. Un día después, la Policía Nacional detuvo a un joven de 18 años como el presunto autor material de los disparos. La principal hipótesis que barajan las autoridades apunta al entorno de un paciente descontento con los resultados de alguna intervención estética previa.
